# CLAUDE.md (.github)

`.github/workflows/dependency-check.yml` asks npm on the 1st of every month (and by hand: `gh workflow run dependency-check.yml`) whether a version in `package-lock.json` has a known vulnerability: `npm audit --package-lock-only`, once with `--omit=dev` (what is in the image) and once for everything, nothing installed. `.github/scripts/dependency-report.ts` turns the two results into one issue with the label `dependency-check` (opened on the first finding, rewritten and commented on by each later run, closed by the first run that finds nothing): each package with its severity, the advisories, the dependency of package.json that brings it in (`comesWith` resolves names through the lockfile the way Node does) and the fix. The script is one file with only Node's own imports, because the workflow runs it with plain `node` (Node 24 runs TypeScript whose types can simply be erased): no import from `src/`, no enum, no `.js` specifier of a `.ts` file. Advisory texts are outside data in a public issue, so `plain` keeps a title from mentioning anyone, pointing at an issue, linking or carrying markup (a zero-width space after `@`, `#`, `<`, `&`), names go into code spans, a link is only made to github.com/advisories, and a command is only written from a name and version that look like one. A result that is not an audit (npm prints its errors as JSON too; npm's own count must match the table) is no report and fails the run, so "could not check" never looks like "nothing found"; the issue step refuses to act without a count. `test/dependency-report.test.ts` also runs the script the way the workflow does. The fix is usually `npm audit fix`, then the typecheck and the tests.
